djr-f324.text: Qui fit Maecenas ut nemo quam sibi sortem, seu ratio dederit, seu sors adjecerit, illa contentus vivat, &c

translations.note: These are the opening lines of Horace, Satires 1.1. The standard text reads 'seu fors obiecerit' ('or chance has thrown in his way'), where Burton has 'seu sors adjecerit'. The quotation breaks off before 'laudet diversa sequentis' ('but praises those who follow other ways'), which is the point Burton illustrates in his main text. Burton gives only 'Hor.' with no locus.
translations.text: How comes it, Maecenas, that no one lives content with the lot that either reason has given him or chance has added, etc.

translations.note: Horace, Satires 1.1, opening, quoted with slight rearrangement ('quam sibi sortem' for 'illa quam sibi sortem'); truncated with &c. Burton's English at the anchor covers only the following gist, loosely.

burton_span.exact: Princes commend a private life, private men itch after honour

translations.text: How comes it, Maecenas, that no one lives content with the lot that reason gave him or chance threw in his way?

djr-f387.text: Bellum quasi bellua & ad omnia scelera furor immissus

translations.literal: War as if a beast and a fury sent in to all crimes
translations.note: The play is etymological: bellum ('war') is linked with bellua ('wild beast'). The construction of 'ad omnia scelera furor immissus' is a little loose. It is not clear whether this sidenote quotes Gerbelius, whom Burton names in the main text.
translations.text: War, a wild beast as it were, and a fury let loose to commit every crime.

translations.note: Wordplay: bellum (war) is derived, as by a false etymology, from bellua (beast). Burton's English only says war is an abominable thing, so it does not render this.
translations.text: War is so called as if from beast, and a fury let loose to every crime.
